items.title: AIエージェントのガバナンスとは？構築6ステップと社内規程・体制の作り方
items.description: 部署ごとにAIエージェントが増え、監査部門から「誰が権限を承認し、誰が止めるのか」と問われて答えに詰まっていないでしょうか。本記事では、 AIエージェントのガバナンスで決めるべき6つの要素と、体制づくりから社内規程までの構築手順 を、公的ガイドラインに沿って解説します。 Microsoft 365 Copilotのエージェントや、Difyで作った社内エージェントが、気づけば部署ごとに動いている。生成AIの利用ガイドラインは作ったものの、メール送信やファイル更新まで自動で行う前提には対応していない。情シスやDX推進の担当者は、このような状況で統制ルールづくりを求められがちです。 AIエージェントのガバナンスとは、 エージェントの権限・責任・停止手段を組織として定め、継続的に監督する仕組み です。曖昧なまま展開すると、誤操作が起きたときに責任の所在を説明できず、統制を急に厳しくすれば現場はシャドーAIに流れます。 本記事では、従来のAIガバナンスとの違いを押さえたうえで、決めるべき6要素と6ステップの構築手順を中心に解説します。AI事業者ガイドライン第1.2版など、2026年の最新動向も整理しました。 読み終えるころには、 社内規程と導入審査の叩き台を作り、経営や監査からの問いに根拠をもって答えられる状態 になっているはずです。 AIエージェントのガバナンスとは AIエージェントのガバナンスを理解するには、以下の3つの観点で整理するとわかりやすくなります。 AIエージェントのガバナンスの定義 従来のAIガバナンスとの違い セキュリティ対策や運用管理との違い 違いを押さえておくと、既存の規程に何を足せばよいかが見えてきます。 AIエージェントのガバナンスの定義 AIエージェントのガバナンスとは、 エージェントに「何をどこまで任せ、誰が責任を持ち、どう止めるか」を組織として決めて監督する仕組み です。 総務省・経済産業省の「AI事業者ガイドライン（第1.2版）」は、AIエージェントを定義しています。特定の目標を達成するために環境を感知し、自律的に行動するAIシステムという位置づけです。自律的に行動する以上、出力の正しさだけでなく、行動の範囲と責任を管理する必要があります。 具体的には、以下のような取り決めがガバナンスの対象です。 エージェントが接続できるシステムと操作できる範囲 導入を承認する人と、日々の挙動に責任を持つ人 人間の確認を必須にする操作と、記録として残す情報 問題が起きたときの停止と復旧の手順 これらを文書と仕組みの両面で決めておけば、現場は迷わずエージェントを使え、管理部門は説明責任を果たせます。 従来のAIガバナンスとの違い 従来のAIガバナンスとの最大の違いは、 統制の対象が「出力」から「行動」に移る 点です。 ChatGPTのような対話型の生成AIでは、回答を読んだ人間が使うかどうかを判断します。一方、AIエージェントは回答を作るだけでなく、メール送信やデータ更新といった操作まで自ら実行します。 観点 従来のAIガバナンス AIエージェントのガバナンス 主な統制対象 出力の正確性・公平性 実行する操作と権限 人間の関与 出力を読んで人間が判断 人間を介さず複数の操作が連続 主なリスク 誤情報・偏り・著作権 誤操作・権限の悪用・連鎖的な障害 必要な記録 入力と出力 ツール呼び出し・参照データ・実行結果 止め方 利用をやめればよい 実行中の処理を止める仕組みが必要 この違いを踏まえると、既存の生成AIガイドラインに 権限・承認・停止のルールを追加する ことが、AIエージェントのガバナンスの出発点になります。 セキュリティ対策や運用管理との違い AIエージェントのガバナンスは、セキュリティ対策や運用管理の 上位にある「決める仕組み」 です。 セキュリティ対策は、プロンプトインジェクションや情報漏えいといった脅威を技術的に防ぐ取り組みを指します。運用管理は、ログ監視や品質評価など、稼働中のエージェントを日々見守る業務です。 これに対してガバナンスは、どの脅威をどこまで許容するか、誰が運用の責任を負うかといった方針と権限を定めます。たとえば「顧客へのメール送信は課長承認を必須にする」と決めるのがガバナンスで、承認フローをシステムに実装するのがセキュリティや運用の役割です。 役割の違いを整理しておけば、情シス・法務・業務部門のどこが何を担うかで議論が空回りしにくくなります。 AIエージェントのガバナンスが今求められる3つの理由 AIエージェントのガバナンスが急いで求められている理由は以下の3つです。 エージェントの判断がそのまま業務の実行になるから 責任の所在が曖昧なまま導入が広がっているから 国内外でエージェント向けのルール整備が進んでいるから いずれも経営層や監査部門に必要性を説明するときの根拠として使えます。 エージェントの判断がそのまま業務の実行になるから 1つ目の理由は、 AIエージェントの誤りが、人間の確認を経ずに業務上の事故になる ためです。 AI事業者ガイドライン第1.2版の別添では、自律的に動くAIエージェントが人間の意図しない商品の注文やファイル削除を行う可能性を指摘しています。外部システムとの連携を通じて攻撃を受け、内部データが漏えいするおそれにも触れています。 対話型AIなら誤った回答は読んだ人が気づけますが、エージェントは誤った判断のまま次の操作へ進みます。 権限が広いほど、1回の誤りがそのまま被害の大きさに直結 します。 事前に任せる範囲と確認ポイントを決めておけば、誤りが起きても被害を小さく抑えられます。 責任の所在が曖昧なまま導入が広がっているから 2つ目の理由は、 エージェントの作成が容易になり、管理されないエージェントが社内に増えている ためです。 Microsoft Copilot StudioやDifyを使えば、業務部門の担当者でもエージェントを作れます。その結果、誰が作り、どのシステムに接続し、誰が保守しているかを情シスが把握できない状態が生まれやすくなります。 作成者が異動や退職をすると、権限を持ったまま持ち主のいないエージェントが残ります。事故が起きたとき「誰の責任か」を説明できなければ、経営や監査からの信頼を失うでしょう。 Gartnerは、エージェント型AIプロジェクトの40%超が2027年末までに中止されると予測しています。要因として挙げたのは、コストの高騰、事業価値の不明確さ、不十分なリスク管理です。 責任と統制を先に設計することが、投資を無駄にしない条件 といえます。 出典： Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027（Gartner） 国内外でエージェント向けのルール整備が進んでいるから 3つ目の理由は、 2026年に入り、AIエージェントを名指しした公的ルールが相次いで出ている ためです。 主な動きは以下のとおりです。 2026年1月：シンガポールがAIエージェント向けのガバナンス枠組みを公表 2026年3月：総務省・経済産業省がAI事業者ガイドライン第1.2版でAIエージェントへの対応を追記 2026年5月：EUが高リスクAIの義務の適用時期を見直す合意に到達 日本のガイドラインは法的拘束力を持ちませんが、取引先や監査法人がAI管理体制を確認する際の基準として参照されます。 海外拠点や海外顧客を持つ企業は、EU AI Actへの対応も視野に入れる必要 があります。 公的ルールに沿って体制を整えておけば、外部から説明を求められたときに根拠をもって回答できます。各ルールの詳細は後半の見出しで解説します。 AIエージェントのガバナンスで決めるべき6つの要素 AIエージェントのガバナンスでは、以下の6つの要素をエージェントごとに決めます。 自律度：どこまで任せるか 権限：何にアクセスさせるか ID：エージェントを誰に紐づけるか 承認：どこで人間が判断するか 記録：何をログに残すか 停止：どう止めて元に戻すか 6つのうち1つでも欠けると、事故が起きたときに原因の特定や責任の説明ができなくなります。 自律度：どこまで任せるか 最初に決めるのは、 エージェントに人間の確認なしでどこまで実行させるか という自律度です。 自律度によって必要な統制の強さが変わるため、すべてのエージェントに同じルールを当てはめると、過剰か不足のどちらかになります。たとえば以下の4段階で区分すると判断しやすくなります。 提案のみ：下書きや候補を作り、実行は人間が行う 承認後に実行：人間が承認した操作だけを実行する 範囲内で自動実行：決められた範囲は自動で実行し、人間が事後に確認する 自律実行：目標だけを与え、手段の選択も任せる 導入初期は1〜2段階目から始め、実績を見ながら段階を上げるのが安全です。 段階ごとに求める統制を規程に書いておけば 、新しいエージェントの審査も迷わず進められます。 権限：何にアクセスさせるか 権限では、 業務に必要な最小限のシステムとデータだけにアクセスさせる ことを原則にします。 エージェントに与えた権限は、そのまま誤操作や乗っ取りが起きたときの被害範囲になります。作成者本人の権限をそのまま流用すると、本来不要な人事データや経理システムまで触れる状態になりかねません。 決めるべき項目は以下のとおりです。 接続を許可するシステム・SaaS・API 参照のみか、更新・削除・外部送信まで許すか 扱ってよいデータの機密区分 権限の有効期限と見直しの頻度 「参照中心から始め、更新・削除・外部送信は個別に審査する」と決めておくと、権限の付けすぎを防ぎながら導入を進められます。 ID：エージェントを誰に紐づけるか IDの要素では、 エージェントごとに固有のIDを発行し、責任者となる人間を紐づけます 。 複数のエージェントが共通のサービスアカウントで動いていると、ログを見てもどのエージェントの操作か区別できません。人間の社員と同じように、エージェントにも「誰か」がわかる身元が必要です。 Microsoftの「Microsoft Entra Agent ID」は、エージェントに固有のIDを割り当て、スポンサーと呼ばれる責任者を設定できます。Google Cloudも、エージェントごとに固有のIDを発行する「Agent Identity」を提供しています。 責任者を紐づけておけば、作成者が異動したときに引き継ぎ先を決める運用も回せます。 持ち主のいないエージェントを残さない ことが、統制の土台になります。 承認：どこで人間が判断するか 承認の要素では、 取り消せない操作や影響の大きい操作の前に、人間の判断を必ず挟む ポイントを決めます。 すべての操作に承認を求めると、確認作業が形だけになり、エージェントを使う意味も薄れます。承認は、失敗したときに元に戻せない操作に絞るのが現実的です。 人間の承認を必須にすべき操作の例は以下のとおりです。 顧客や取引先など社外への送信 支払い・発注・契約などお金や法的効果が伴う操作 データの削除や本番環境の設定変更 権限の付与や変更 承認者と承認期限まで決めておけば、承認待ちで業務が止まる事態も防げます。 記録：何をログに残すか 記録の要素では、 エージェントが「何を見て、何を判断し、何を実行したか」を後から追えるログ を残すことを決めます。 入力と出力だけでは、エージェントがどのツールをどの順番で呼び出したかがわかりません。事故の原因調査や監査対応には、行動の過程まで含めた記録が必要です。 残すべき項目は以下のとおりです。 エージェントIDと、指示を出した利用者 参照したデータや文書 呼び出したツールと引数、実行結果 人間の承認の有無と承認者 ログには個人情報が含まれやすいため、 マスキングの方法と保存期間も合わせて決めておきましょう 。記録が揃っていれば、監査で問われたときに事実をもとに説明できます。 停止：どう止めて元に戻すか 停止の要素では、 異常が起きたときに誰が、どの手段で、どこまで止めるか を事前に決めます。 AIエージェントは人間より速く操作を繰り返すため、異常に気づいてから止め方を考えていては被害が広がります。停止の権限を持つ人が不在で対応が遅れるケースも想定しておく必要があります。 決めておくべき項目は以下のとおりです。 停止を判断できる人と、その代行者 エージェントの無効化や認証情報の失効など、止める手段 停止を発動する条件 データや設定を元に戻す手順と、関係者への連絡先 停止手順を一度訓練しておけば、本番の事故でも慌てずに被害を最小限に抑えられます。 AIエージェントのガバナンス体制と役割分担 AIエージェントのガバナンス体制は、以下の4者で役割を分担して作ります。 経営層とAIガバナンス委員会の役割 エージェントオーナーの役割 情シス・セキュリティ部門の役割 法務・内部監査部門の役割 情シスだけに任せると統制が技術に偏り、業務部門だけに任せるとリスク判断が甘くなるため、分担を明文化することが重要です。 経営層とAIガバナンス委員会の役割 経営層とAIガバナンス委員会は、 AIエージェント活用の方針と、許容するリスクの水準を決める 役割を担います。 どこまでの自律実行を認めるか、どの業務には使わないかといった判断は、部門単位では決めきれません。全社の方針として決める場がないと、部門ごとに基準がばらつきます。 AIガバナンス委員会は、情シス・法務・リスク管理・主要な業務部門の責任者で構成し、四半期ごとなど定期的に開くのが一般的です。高リスクに分類したエージェントの導入可否や、規程の改定もこの場で承認します。 経営層が委員会の決定に責任を持つ形にしておくと、 現場は「会社として認められた使い方」として安心して活用 できます。 エージェントオーナーの役割 エージェントオーナーとは、 個々のエージェントの業務成果と日々の挙動に責任を持つ業務部門の担当者 です。 エージェントがどの業務で何をすべきかを最もよく知っているのは、実際にその業務を担う部門です。作った人が責任を持つのではなく、部門として責任者を指名しておくと、異動や退職があっても管理が途切れません。 エージェントオーナ

items.title: AIエージェントを比較！業務向け主要15サービスの違いと稟議用評価シート
items.description: AIエージェントの比較記事を読むほど候補が増え、自社に合う製品を絞り込めない。本記事では、 3種類に分けた主要15サービスの比較表、迷いやすい製品同士の違い、稟議に使える評価シート を、2026年11月時点の公式情報をもとに解説します。 AIエージェントの比較表を開くと、汎用型のChatGPT、構築基盤のCopilot Studio、開発ツールのClaude Codeが同じ表に並んでいることがよくあります。種類の違う製品を一つの表で比べても、自社に合う1つは決まりません。 比較の物差しを持たずに選ぶと、既存基盤との連携や課金単位の違いに導入後に気づき、追加開発や想定外のコストが発生します。反対に、種類を決めてから同じ土俵で比べれば、候補は2〜3製品まで絞れます。 本記事では、AIエージェントを汎用型・構築基盤型・開発特化型に分けた比較表と、料金を課金単位で比べる方法、稟議にそのまま使える評価シートを中心に解説します。 読み終えるころには、 候補製品を絞り込み、「なぜこの製品か」を根拠付きで説明できる状態 になっているでしょう。 AIエージェントを比較する5つの軸 AIエージェントを比較するときに見るべき軸は以下の5つです。 自律性：どこまで任せられるか 連携性：既存基盤とつながるか ガバナンス：権限と監査ログを管理できるか 料金体系：何に対して課金されるか 日本語とサポート：国内で運用できるか 月額料金だけで比べると、導入後に権限設計や連携開発で想定外の工数が発生するため、5軸をそろえて確認しましょう。 自律性：どこまで任せられるか 自律性は、 人の指示なしにどこまで作業を進められるか を見る軸です。 同じ「AIエージェント」でも、指示ごとに1つの作業をこなす製品から、計画を立てて複数のツールを操作し、完成物まで仕上げる製品まで幅があります。 たとえばChatGPT WorkやClaudeは、調べものから資料作成までを一続きで進めます。一方でCopilot Studioのような構築基盤では、どこまで自動で動かすかを自社で設計します。 あわせて、 重要な操作の前に人の承認を挟めるか も確認しましょう。n8nは、機密性の高いツールを実行する前に承認を求める設定ができます。 自律性と承認の仕組みを分けて評価すれば、任せる範囲を段階的に広げる導入計画を立てやすくなります。 連携性：既存基盤とつながるか 連携性は、 社内のメール・ファイル・業務システムに接続できるか を見る軸です。 AIエージェントは社内データに触れて初めて業務で役に立ちます。既存基盤と相性の悪い製品を選ぶと、SSO連携やデータ接続の追加開発が必要になります。 Microsoft 365を全社で使っているならMicrosoft 365 CopilotやCopilot Studio、Salesforceが基幹ならAgentforceが自然な候補です。Gemini EnterpriseはGoogle Workspaceに加え、SharePointやTeamsのコネクタも用意しています。 自社の基盤から候補を逆算すると、比較対象を最初から2〜3製品に絞れます。 ガバナンス：権限と監査ログを管理できるか ガバナンスは、 誰が何を実行したかを管理者が把握・制御できるか を見る軸です。 AIエージェントはファイル編集や外部サービスの操作など、実際の作業を実行します。チャットAIより誤操作の影響が大きいため、管理機能の差が導入可否を左右します。 確認したい項目は以下の4つです。 SSO・SCIMで社内アカウントと連携できるか 監査ログで操作履歴を取得できるか 入力データがモデルの学習に使われないか 部署やロールごとに利用範囲を制限できるか 注意したいのは、同じ製品でもプランで差が出る点です。ClaudeやDifyでは、監査ログはEnterpriseプランに限られます。必要な管理要件から最低限のプランを先に決めておくと、料金比較の前提がぶれません。 料金体系：何に対して課金されるか 料金は、月額の金額よりも 「何に対して課金されるか」 で比べます。 AIエージェントの課金単位は、ユーザー数・クレジット・実行回数・計算資源などに分かれます。利用規模によって、安く見えた製品の総額が逆転することも珍しくありません。 たとえばClaudeのTeamプランは1席ごとの席課金、n8nはワークフローの実行回数、Amazon Bedrock AgentCoreはvCPU時間などの従量課金です。 課金単位をそろえて試算すれば、利用が広がった後のコストまで経営層に説明できます。具体的な試算方法は後半の「AIエージェントの料金は課金単位で比較する」で解説します。 日本語とサポート：国内で運用できるか 日本語対応は、 管理画面・出力・料金表示の3つ に分けて確認します。 回答が日本語で出ても、管理画面が英語のみだと設定やトラブル対応を担う情シスの負担が増えます。料金がドル建てなら、為替による予算のぶれも考慮が必要です。 たとえばDifyの公式ドキュメントでは、管理画面の表示言語は英語・簡体字中国語・繁体字中国語と案内されています。料金ではMicrosoftとSalesforceが円建て価格を公開している一方、OpenAI・Anthropic・Manusはドル表記です。 参考： 個人アカウント管理（Dify） 日本語で運用できる範囲を把握しておけば、社内マニュアルの作成や問い合わせ対応の工数まで見積もれます。 AIエージェントは3種類に分けて比較する AIエージェントは、使い方の違いから以下の3種類に分かれます。 汎用型：個人の業務をそのまま任せる 構築基盤型：自社専用のエージェントを作る 開発特化型：コーディングを任せる 種類をまたいで比べると「高機能だが自社の用途には合わない製品」を選ぶ原因になるため、まず自社に必要な種類を決めましょう。 汎用型：個人の業務をそのまま任せる 汎用型は、 契約してすぐ社員が使える完成品のAIエージェント です。 チャット画面で依頼を書くだけで、情報収集・資料作成・ブラウザ操作などを自律的に進めます。開発が不要なため、全社展開の最初の一手に向いています。 本記事で比較するのは、ChatGPT Work、Claude、Microsoft 365 Copilot、Manusの4つです。いずれも文書・表・スライドといった完成物まで作れる点が共通しています。 ただし、決まった業務フローへの組み込みや、社外向けの窓口対応には向きません。 まず汎用型で社員の利用習慣を作ると 、自社専用のエージェントが必要な業務も見えてきます。 構築基盤型：自社専用のエージェントを作る 構築基盤型は、 自社の業務やデータに合わせてエージェントを作る土台 です。 社内問い合わせ対応や営業の案件管理など、決まった業務フローに組み込むには、接続するデータや判断のルールを自社で設計する必要があります。 作り方の難易度は製品によって異なり、以下の3段階に分かれます。 ノーコード中心：Gemini Enterprise、Dify ローコード中心：Microsoft Copilot Studio、Salesforce Agentforce、n8n コードが必要：Amazon Bedrock AgentCore 作り込みの度合いと社内の開発体制を照らし合わせれば、内製で進めるか外部に委託するかまで判断できます。 開発特化型：コーディングを任せる 開発特化型は、 コードの読解・修正・テスト・プルリクエスト作成を任せるAIエージェント です。 リポジトリ全体を読み、複数のファイルを編集してコマンドを実行します。汎用型よりも開発作業の深い部分まで入り込める点が特徴です。 本記事ではClaude Code、OpenAI Codex、GitHub Copilot、Cursor、Devinの5つを比較します。ターミナルで動くもの、エディタに組み込まれたもの、クラウドで並列に動くものと、作業する場所が製品ごとに異なります。 利用者は開発部門に限られるため、全社向けの汎用型とは別の予算・別の基準で比べましょう。 評価軸を分けておけば 、全社導入と開発ツールの稟議を並行して進められます。 主要AIエージェント15サービスの比較表 主要15サービスを、種類ごとに以下の3つの表で比較します。 汎用型AIエージェントの比較表 構築基盤型AIエージェントの比較表 開発特化型AIエージェントの比較表 items.title: How a Kenyan Startup Is Rethinking AI for Small Businesses
items.description: The first time Mutembei Kariuki thought about how AI models could work in Kenya, his home country, was in 2019. He was attending a conference at the University of Tokyo on the future of AI, and kept hearing about how this technology was going to transform the world. “But nobody mentioned Africa at all,” he says. Even then—before AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic had launched their chatbots to the public—Kariuki could see significant obstacles to AI adoption in Africa. Internet access was slow and unequal, computing resources for training models were scarce, and there was little high-quality, structured training data. Most people, meanwhile, reached the internet through outdated, low-memory cellphones rather than computers or high-end phones. Together with co-founders Jude Mwenda and Stephanie Njerenga , Kariuki created Fastagger , a start-up that builds AI models that can run offline and on low-power cellphones. Its first big product, Auni, is a business intelligence assistant that launched in 2024; it got a big push when it was integrated into the business app of M-Pesa , Kenya’s largest mobile money service. Since then, about 6,000 businesses have signed up. Auni helps small and medium businesses like barbershops, restaurants, and small manufacturers analyze their transaction data and gives them marketing recommendations. Peter Chege, owner of a salon and barbershop in Nairobi, started using Auni last year. Before that, he recorded all his sales on paper. “We were not able to translate that information into a graph,” he says. Now, the app helps him identify his busiest days and hours, as well as his loyal customers. If a regular customer stops coming, for example, he can send a personalized message encouraging them to return. Fastagger is part of an emerging effort to build AI around the technological realities of users in developing economies, rather than adapting products designed for wealthier markets. In Fastagger’s case, that meant finding a way to make their models work despite inexpensive phones, unreliable internet connections, and business records that may consist of little more than mobile-money transactions. Designing AI for Kenya’s Small Businesses Before developing Auni, Kariuki and his co-founders started by tackling the problem of data availability for AI training. They asked themselves: “How do we get Africa to catch up fast? How do we create training data fast enough, and then how do we actually get it into people’s hands fast enough?” Mutembei Kariuki cofounded Fastagger to develop AI systems that can run offline and on basic phones. Afrikanna Production/Microsoft They decided to focus on mobile phones, and specifically on mobile money apps. With more than 80 percent of Kenya’s adults using them, they offer a rich source of data. One of Fastagger’s first steps was to adapt an open-source optical character recognition (OCR) model to read financial statements produced by mobile money apps. Existing models struggled with the low quality of the PDFs, which had unfamiliar formatting and sometimes contained stamps and errors. And because Fastagger’s prospective users often had unreliable internet connections, they made sure key steps, like organizing the extracted data into tables, could run on-device. Once they had a model that could process these documents, they began exploring how that structured financial data could help businesses. They spent entire days watching small-business owners work and interact with their customers. One challenge quickly became clear: Owners had little time or resources to think beyond day-to-day operations. “They are standing up the whole day cutting hair,” Kariuki says of salon owners, who are now among Auni’s main users. “You have to think about that dynamic of the user journey, and how they live, and what will be going on in the background.” The Fastagger app helps salon owner Peter Chege better manage his time and keep track of loyal customers. Afrikanna Production/Microsoft For Chege, one of Auni’s biggest benefits was helping him manage his time. A simple chart showed him that mornings were his slowest hours, so he realized that he could run errands then or keep fewer barbers in the shop until around 1 p.m., when business picked up. The founders also saw how much time businesses spent on manual processes and how automation could simplify those tasks. At a fish restaurant in Nairobi, for example, identifying loyal customers to offer them discounts required going through SMS sales receipts one by one, a tedious task that rendered client-retention marketing impractical. Now, with the help of Auni, the restaurant identifies its top customers automatically and offers them discounts. Some of Auni’s functions—such as reading sales statements, analyzing data, and visualizing results—can happen offline on low-cost phones, without making cloud queries. These functions involve both AI tools and conventional software; for example, standard OCR software extracts the text and a small neural network identifies how each document is structured. More detailed analyses and answering questions about the data, however, require an internet connection. Daniel Björkegren , an economist at Columbia University who studies AI’s implications for developing economies, says sub-Saharan Africa’s prevalence of basic phones rather than smartphones and computers could open the door to different kinds of AI use. “The history of technology should suggest that this is not going to be people running Claude Code or Codex on their laptop,” he says. “You will have people like that, but for much of the population, we’re going to have to figure out different usage modalities.” How Local Needs Are Shaping AI Despite Auni’s integration into M-Pesa, Fastagger remains a small startup. It has received support from Google, Microsoft, and NVIDIA accelerator programs, but still has just three employees: Kariuki, Mwenda and Njerenga, the original founders. items.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
items.description: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators . Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage. An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay. In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood. A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms). Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically. The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer. A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?” Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says. During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right. There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers. Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment. Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.” One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should. It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. items.title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
items.description: arXiv:2610.37826v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

items.title: Turing LLM Post-Training: Calibrated Distillation and Efficient Dynamic-MoE Execution
items.description: arXiv:2610.39876v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study post-training for dynamically routed mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, focusing on integrating independently optimized specialists while keeping consolidation efficient. Our approach combines calibrated multi-teacher on-policy distillation (C-MOPD), which matches each selected teacher on a local Top-$K$ support with teacher-wise loss normalization and clipping, with an execution path that uses post-capacity bounded-width dispatch, final-route replay, and asynchronous rollout--training overlap. On Turing-20B-A2B, the selected model achieves a four-domain normalized integration score of 0.9988 and retains at least 90.16\% of the measured specialist gain in every domain. At matched $K=32$, the full calibration objective scores 0.9962, compared with 0.9724 without calibration and 0.9834 without clipping. At a matched 8K response cap, the model exceeds both shared SFT and Qwen3-8B on all four reasoning-enabled mathematics and code benchmarks (unweighted mean: 85.92, versus 80.33 for Qwen3-8B and 74.21 for SFT), and improves over SFT on ten of twelve broader evaluation metrics. In a PPU-based profile, the combined execution configuration reduces consolidation step time from 398.7 to 139.3 seconds, an observed 2.86$\times$ speedup over serial execution. These results demonstrate strong specialist integration alongside more efficient consolidation, while reflecting the complete training and execution framework rather than any single component.

items.title: NECA: Neighbor Event Curve Augmentation for Multi-Horizon ICU Deterioration Prediction
items.description: arXiv:2610.40420v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Early prediction of ICU organ dysfunction events supports timely clinical monitoring and intervention, but estimating short-term organ-specific risk from early ICU records remains challenging due to irregular measurements, heterogeneous clinical variables, and the need to predict risk across multiple future horizons. Existing supervised models usually treat each patient as an isolated sample and do not explicitly use the observed event timing of similar historical patients. We propose Neighbor Event-Curve Augmentation (NECA), a model-agnostic method that retrieves training-set patients with similar early-window profiles and converts their subsequent organ dysfunction event onset times into cumulative event-curve features over 6h, 12h, 24h, and 42h. These features are concatenated with the original patient representation and used by standard downstream predictors. On PhysioNet 2012 and a 4,000-stay MIMIC-IV subset, NECA improves average PR-AUC and ROC-AUC across four organ dysfunction event tasks and seven supervised learners. The largest gain appears for neurological dysfunction events, where task-level average PR-AUC increases from 0.461 to 0.557 on PhysioNet 2012. Ablations show that clinically meaningful retrieval and horizon-specific neighbor risk drive most of the improvement, while the full cumulative curve adds task-dependent temporal context. These results support similar-patient event timing as a structured temporal risk signal for ICU organ dysfunction event prediction. The source code will be publicly released upon acceptance of this paper.

items.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.21561v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

items.title: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs, Exposure, and the Trust Trap in Multi-Relational Graph Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.37239v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-relational graph detectors learn from clean data how much to trust each relation, but an adversary pays a different price to manipulate each relation and each action; taking such costs as given, we ask when using a relation is worse than ignoring it. Our first main result proves that degree gating strictly beats every selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate, and that this window is sharp; on real graphs, validated gating gains exactly on the relations that meet these conditions and nowhere else. Our second shows that a per-node exposure bound, which extends to message passing, tells a platform which relation to harden: exposure per unit cost, computed without any attack, picks the relation whose hardening raises the exact trap threshold most in 15 of 16 cases, against at most 7 for informativeness, cheapness, or an analysis with equal edit costs. Supporting tools give exact worst cases for linear relational models, certified brackets for R-GCN and tree ensembles, and a finite-sample guarantee for adversarial validation, under which clean-trained graph detectors fall below their graph-free counterparts in 58 of 90 settings on six graphs. A selection protocol built on these results is never significantly worse than ignoring the graph; with at most four relations it mostly abstains, as validation alone would, and its cost-aware proposals help when relations are many, so far shown on synthetic graphs. Without cost information, the safe choice is to abstain.

items.title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.41291v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

items.title: BlindToChange: AI Agents Can Find Changes When Asked But Do They Look When Needed?
items.description: arXiv:2610.41435v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given that AI agents can search the web broadly and deeply in real time, it is tempting to conclude that their outputs account for recent world events. We show that this conclusion does not hold in practice. While agents can search and easily find recent changes, the correctness of their responses depends on whether they search and what they search for. Popular agentic search benchmarks like BrowseComp cannot expose failures wherein agents do not recognize their own assumptions that should be verified, since these benchmarks explicitly state what needs to be found. In contrast, many user requests state only the final information need (e.g., an itinerary for a trip), leaving the agent to discover relevant changes (e.g., the temporary closure of a museum) and account for their consequences. To highlight such gaps, we introduce BlindToChange, a benchmark that measures whether agents proactively discover recent events that affect their responses. Our benchmark comprises requests for recommendations where an obvious candidate is no longer applicable due to a recent real-world event. These events are drawn automatically from Wikidata, allowing BlindToChange to be periodically refreshed. Strikingly, we find a big gap -- as high as 27.5 points, even at high reasoning effort -- in systems' performance, when the recent event is not explicitly mentioned compared to when we ask about it directly. Analyzing search trajectories, we learn that more than half of the failures can be attributed to the fact that agents do not directly search to verify whether a relevant fact has changed. Our benchmark highlights, and tracks, a new axis of progress, wherein systems account for recent information that is not explicitly mentioned in the user request.

items.title: KEEPER: Learning Control-Sufficient Textual Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.41482v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.

items.title: Sparse Text Diffusion under Dual Budgets: Context Connectivity and Expert Activation
items.description: arXiv:2610.41487v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.

items.title: When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
items.description: arXiv:2610.41661v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model's weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. Prior work has measured these changes only through coarse signals such as perplexity. In this work, we show that steering systematically produces significant changes in discourse dimensions of the generated text, such as its formality, use of evidence, and ambiguity. We present a way of countering this by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. This intervention restores about 78% of the unintended discourse changes while preserving the intended steering behavior in about 93% of the generations.

items.title: SimXAI: A Simple Drop-in Layer Increases Interaction Quality and Understanding in Conversational XAI
items.description: arXiv:2610.41856v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use GUS-style architectures with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template-based response generation. While faithful to the underlying XAI methods, these pipelines are hard to adapt and often struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. We present SimXAI, a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Rather than a standalone agent, SimXAI serves as a modular interface that enables conversational access to external XAI resources. We further introduce an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness, and contextualization. Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while better handling context-dependent requests. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turn. Overall, SimXAI improves GUS-based design while preserving faithfulness and improving conversational quality.

items.title: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
items.description: arXiv:2610.41951v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.

items.title: CRoS: Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs Improves Accuracy and Reasoning Faithfulness
items.description: arXiv:2610.42054v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the standard method for training language models to reason. However, RLVR typically relies solely on outcome correctness, which does not guarantee that the CoT causally contributes to the final answer. Without this connection, outcome rewards may fail to reinforce high-quality reasoning. Existing causality metrics assess CoT causality by perturbing the CoT, such as deleting reasoning steps or injecting errors, and measuring changes in the final answer. However, these perturbations inevitably alter information in each step. Consequently, high causality scores may reflect sensitivity to information changes introduced by perturbation rather than true causality. Such confounding effects further induce undesirable reasoning behaviors when these metrics are used as training rewards, including generating less informative CoTs and reducing exploration and self-correction. To address this problem, we propose CRoS (Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs), a novel CoT causality metric that perturbs the order of reasoning steps without altering content, thereby preserving information within each step. On Reasoning Gym with Gemma-3-4B, CRoS outperforms existing causality and outcome rewards in out-of-domain accuracy, CoT quality, and CoT faithfulness. Specifically, CRoS achieves 46.8% accuracy on five unseen logic and games datasets, outperforming the strongest baseline (43.8%). It also achieves better CoT quality, consistently outperforming baselines in CoT-Pass@K from K=1 to 128, averaging 43.4% vs. 41.4%. For CoT faithfulness, CRoS achieves a hint acknowledgment score of 34.0% vs. 20.2%.

items.title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
items.description: arXiv:2610.42112v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.

items.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
items.description: arXiv:2610.41172v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.

items.title: ProSearch: Benchmarking Multi-Constraint Protocol Retrieval in Experimental Science
items.description: arXiv:2610.41396v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In AI for Science scenarios, experimental design and method reproduction require retrieving protocols that satisfy multiple interdependent constraints, yet existing benchmarks lack systematic evaluation of this capability. To address this gap, we introduce ProSearch, a benchmark for multi-constraint protocol retrieval in experimental science. ProSearch has three key features: (1) realism, with queries grounded in real experimental records and expert-defined templates; (2) complexity, with 60 experimental fields and their dependencies; and (3) diagnosticity, with 3-5 explicit constraints per query, including numerical and negation constraints. We construct ProSearch through LLM-based extraction, data-driven constraint selection, controlled query generation, and evidence-based relevance validation. The resulting benchmark contains 1,515 queries across six experimental science domains. We conduct extensive experiments on ProSearch with 19 representative retrievers and complementary analyses. The best-performing retriever achieves an average nDCG@10 of only 0.290, which improves to 0.474 with reranking. Structured diagnostic analysis shows that explicit constraint matching provides a strong ranking signal, while manual error analysis identifies joint constraint binding as a key bottleneck. ProSearch provides a testbed for systematically evaluating scientific retrieval systems.

items.title: SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention
items.description: arXiv:2610.41420v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.

items.title: GRIT: Gradient Masking for Visually Misgrounded Tokens in Text-Rich Reasoning
items.description: arXiv:2610.41629v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently been extended to vision-language models (VLMs), yet its effectiveness remains limited for text-rich reasoning tasks. We highlight a key factor contributing to this limitation: models frequently arrive at correct final answers despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate steps. We define this phenomenon as Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR). Because standard RLVR rewards only final-answer correctness, it fails to differentiate between properly grounded and misgrounded reasoning, reinforcing both equally. Through token-level analysis, we reveal that CVMR tokens exhibit distinct attention patterns that differ systematically from well-grounded ones. Based on this observation, we propose GRIT, a training framework that incorporates visual grounding into RLVR to mitigate the impact of CVMR. Furthermore, to address the lack of text-rich reasoning benchmarks that allow for systematic evaluation across text length and reasoning depth, we introduce GRIT-Bench. Experiments demonstrate that GRIT significantly improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.

items.title: Beyond Public Access in LLM Pre-Training Data
items.description: arXiv:2505.00020v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Using a legally obtained dataset of 34 copyrighted O'Reilly Media books (13,962 paragraphs), we apply the DE-COP membership inference attack to test whether OpenAI models show recognition of non-public (pay-walled) content they were not licensed to train on. Our main contribution is examining non-public books, which allows us to consider potential access violations and not just training inclusion. Our results suggest that GPT-4o, OpenAI's more recent and capable model in our sample, exhibits patterns consistent with recognition of non-public books, with an AUROC score of 0.82 (95% bootstrapped CI: 0.60-0.96) -- where above 50% is better than random chance. GPT-3.5 Turbo (trained two years prior) and the smaller GPT-4o Mini both score near chance recognition on non-public data (0.54 and 0.56, respectively). Results are robust to independent paraphrasers (Gemma and Qwen) and leave-one-book-out sensitivity analyses. We also test both GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini, with the same October 2023 training cutoff date, to ensure the model is not simply identifying language shifts over time. These findings support disclosure requirements for pre-training data provenance and formal licensing markets for training content. Results remain preliminary given the small book sample, possible contamination of post-cutoff controls, and differences across models in size, architecture, and training composition.

items.title: Enhancing Safety of Large Language Models via Embedding Space Separation
items.description: arXiv:2603.20206v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Safety alignment does not fully prevent large language models (LLMs) from producing harmful content under adversarial attacks. We observe that existing attack methods typically move harmful embeddings toward regions of harmless embeddings. This motivates us to explore whether increasing the distance between harmful and harmless embeddings can improve the safety of LLMs, since greater separation requires attacks to make larger embedding shifts, which can destroy semantics. We propose Embedding Space Separation (ES2), a fine-tuning method that increases the distance between harmful and harmless embeddings. However, maximizing this distance alone can damage LLMs' capabilities. Thus, we use two regularization losses: an embedding anchor loss keeps harmless embeddings close in direction to those of a frozen base model and a KL-divergence loss keeps output distributions on harmless prompts close to those of the base model. Our experimental results demonstrate that ES2 has excellent defensive performance against various attack methods. LLMs fine-tuned with ES2 retain general capabilities comparable to those of the baseline models, though some performance degradation is observed on certain tasks. Our results indicate that ES2 is an effective way to enhance the safety of large language models, while maintaining comparable performance on general capabilities.

items.title: EvoMemBench: Benchmarking Agent Memory from a Self-Evolving Perspective
items.description: arXiv:2605.18421v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent benchmarks for Large Language Model (LLM) agents mainly evaluate reasoning, planning, and execution. However, memory is also essential for agents, as it enables them to store, update, and retrieve information over time. This ability remains under-evaluated, largely because existing benchmarks do not provide a systematic way to assess memory mechanisms. In this paper, we study agent memory from a self-evolving perspective and introduce EvoMemBench, a unified benchmark organized along two axes: memory scope (in-episode vs. cross-episode) and memory content (knowledge-oriented vs. execution-oriented). We compare 15 representative memory methods with strong long-context baselines under a standardized protocol. Results show that current memory systems are still far from a general solution: long-context baselines remain highly competitive, memory helps most when the current context is insufficient or tasks are difficult, and no single memory form works consistently across all settings. Retrieval-based methods remain strong for knowledge-intensive settings, whereas procedural and long-term memory methods are more effective for execution-oriented tasks when their stored experience matches the task structure. We hope EvoMemBench facilitates future research on more effective memory systems for LLM-based agents. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/DSAIL-Memory/EvoMemBench.

items.title: CogBattery: Human-Referenced Evaluation of Cognitive Task Behavior and Structure in Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2607.24999v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Human cognitive tasks let us compare language models with humans under controlled conditions. Yet a model can reproduce the direction of a human effect while making different errors. CogBattery evaluates 54 open-weight language models on text adaptations of 13 cognitive paradigms, comparing each with human data from its source study. Like humans, models respond more to n-back lures than to controls, yet they make far more false alarms on ordinary non-targets. Most models' reported confidence separates correct from incorrect answers less well than humans' does, and most always choose the same wager, including models that classify accurately. These patterns span many model families. Across tasks, model scores share two dimensions. The first is closely tied to scale, yet larger models are not consistently closer to humans. Predefined cognitive groupings show no reliable predictive advantage over random groupings of the same size. These results show that matching human effect directions does not establish human-like behavior. CogBattery provides condition-level human references for testing errors and confidence reports in new models.

items.title: TamilEOT: A Dataset and Model for Semantic End-of-Turn Detection in Tamil Telephone Speech
items.description: arXiv:2609.05631v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A voice agent must decide, at each pause, whether the speaker has finished or is still thinking. Without a model of the language, systems fall back to a fixed silence timeout: too short, and the agent interrupts; too long, and every turn pays the full wait. We release TamilEOT, to our knowledge the first open dataset and detector for semantic end-of-turn detection in a South Indian language: 18,485 labelled turn boundaries from 116 real Tamil telephone conversations, two audio-only detectors built on Smart Turn v3's architecture, and a turn-level companion set of 4,774 whole turns with their pause structure. On a held-out split of 4,168 clips from 30 unseen calls, accuracy rises from 70.30% zero-shot to 83.71% (8.7 MB) and 86.13% (21 MB); ROC-AUC rises from 0.751 to 0.921. Both run in under 150 ms single-threaded on a laptop CPU. We also report what building it cost. Our rule-derived negative-class labels scored 44.4% against a blind human pass, below chance, because the rule answered a different question than the model is asked; an audio-LLM labeller at 97.5% agreement replaced them for US$5.69. Of six training levers, only encoder capacity moved the result: three identical runs spanned 0.87 accuracy points, the floor below which nothing else here is a finding. Replaying labelled boundaries through the production VAD and streaming adapter costs a further 2.60 points, and 7.8% of boundaries never reach the model at all. Data, weights, code and every negative result are public.

items.title: SOPO: Socratic Guided Policy Optimization for Span-Level Hallucination Detection
items.description: arXiv:2610.32212v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

items.title: Adapting LLM-SC to Living Sacred Heritage: Domain-Specific Extraction, Semantic Networks and Human Evaluation on Pashupatinath Temple Reviews
items.description: arXiv:2610.35685v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) pipelines can turn visitor reviews into structured data, but generic schemes may miss rituals, sacred spaces, cultural restrictions and emotionally mixed experiences at living sacred heritage sites. We adapted the LLM-Social Computing (LLM-SC) framework to Pashupatinath Temple, Nepal, by specifying a 12-type entity taxonomy (four original LLM-SC types plus eight sacred-heritage types), four relation types and nine aspect-sentiment dimensions in a GPT-4o extraction prompt, which was applied to a fixed random sample of 2,500 English-language Tripadvisor reviews from a processed corpus of 3,939. The exports contain 11,286 entity, 6,232 aspect-sentiment and 5,590 relation records, covering 2,485, 2,487 and 2,433 reviews, respectively; the eight added sacred-heritage types account for 64.8% of entity records. Against an adjudicated two-annotator reference for 200 reviews, exact normalized surface-and-type matching gave provisional entity scores of 41.0% precision, 21.8% recall and 28.4% micro-F1. Aspect-presence F1 was 53.6% and end-to-end aspect-plus-polarity F1 was 42.6%. Human adjudication supported 153 of 194 first-listed relation candidates (one per review; 78.9%), a candidate-level rate that does not estimate relation recall or whole-graph precision. The contribution is a culturally grounded, domain-specific adaptation with component-wise human evaluation and explicit reproducibility and generalization limitations.

items.title: Optimizing Anytime Reasoning via Budget Relative Policy Optimization
items.description: arXiv:2505.13438v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scaling test-time compute is crucial for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches typically employ reinforcement learning (RL) to maximize a verifiable reward obtained at the end of reasoning traces. However, such methods optimize only the final performance under a large and fixed token budget, which hinders efficiency in both training and deployment. In this work, we present a novel framework, AnytimeReasoner, to optimize anytime reasoning performance, which aims to improve token efficiency and the flexibility of reasoning under varying token budget constraints. To achieve this, we truncate the complete thinking process to fit within sampled token budgets from a prior distribution, compelling the model to summarize the optimal answer for each truncated thinking for verification. This introduces verifiable dense rewards into the reasoning process, facilitating more effective credit assignment in RL optimization. We then optimize the thinking and summary policies in a decoupled manner to maximize the cumulative reward. Additionally, we introduce a novel variance reduction technique, Budget Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO), to enhance the robustness and efficiency of the learning process when reinforcing the thinking policy. Empirical results in mathematical reasoning tasks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms GRPO across all thinking budgets under various prior distributions, enhancing both training and token efficiency.

items.title: Eroding the Truth-Default: A Causal Analysis of Human Susceptibility to Foundation Model Hallucinations and Disinformation in the Wild
items.description: arXiv:2601.22871v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As foundation models (FMs) approach human-level fluency, distinguishing synthetic from organic content has become a key challenge for Trustworthy Web Intelligence. This paper presents JudgeGPT and RogueGPT, a dual-axis framework that decouples "authenticity" from "attribution" to investigate the mechanisms of human susceptibility. Analyzing 918 evaluations across five FMs (including GPT-4 and Llama-2), we employ Structural Causal Models (SCMs) as a principal framework for formulating testable causal hypotheses about detection accuracy. Contrary to partisan narratives, we find that political orientation shows a negligible association with detection performance ($r=-0.10$). Instead, "fake news familiarity" emerges as a candidate mediator ($r=0.35$), suggesting that exposure may function as adversarial training for human discriminators. We identify a "fluency trap" where GPT-4 outputs (HumanMachineScore: 0.20) bypass Source Monitoring mechanisms, rendering them indistinguishable from human text. These findings suggest that "pre-bunking" interventions should target cognitive source monitoring rather than demographic segmentation to ensure trustworthy information ecosystems.

items.title: Can Humans Tell? A Dual-Axis Study of Human Perception of LLM-Generated News
items.description: arXiv:2604.03755v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Can humans tell whether a news article was written by a person or a large language model (LLM)? We investigate this question using JudgeGPT, a study platform that independently measures source attribution (human vs. machine) and authenticity judgment (legitimate vs. fake) on continuous scales. From 2,318 judgments collected from 1,054 participants across content generated by six LLMs, we report five findings: (1) participants cannot reliably distinguish machine-generated from human-written text (p > .05, Welch's t-test); (2) this inability holds across all tested models, including open-weight models with as few as 7B parameters; (3) self-reported domain expertise predicts judgment accuracy (r = .35, p < .001) whereas political orientation does not (r = -.10, n.s.); (4) clustering reveals distinct response strategies ("Skeptics" vs. "Believers"); and (5) accuracy degrades after approximately 30 sequential evaluations due to cognitive fatigue. The answer, in short, is no: humans cannot reliably tell. These results indicate that user-side detection is not a viable defense and motivate system-level countermeasures such as cryptographic content provenance.

items.title: M$^\star$: Every Task Deserves Its Own Memory Harness
items.description: arXiv:2604.11811v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model agents rely on a memory harness to write, organize, retrieve, and use past experience. A harness that works for one task often fails on another, because conversations, embodied planning, and expert reasoning require different storage and retrieval behavior. To address this limitation, we introduce Mstar, a method that automatically discovers task-optimized memory programs through reflective code evolution. Specifically, Mstar operationalizes a memory harness as an executable Python memory program that defines the Schema, Logic, and Instruction, and optimizes these components jointly. We evaluate Mstar on four tasks covering conversation, embodied planning, and specialized reasoning. Our results demonstrate that Mstar improves performance over existing baselines across all evaluated tasks. Furthermore, the evolved memory programs exhibit structurally distinct processing mechanisms for each evaluated domain. These findings suggest that every task benefits from its own memory harness, and that memory-program search provides a concrete way to discover it.

items.title: A Survey on Long-Term Memory Security in LLM Agents: Attacks, Defenses, and Governance Across the Memory Lifecycle
items.description: arXiv:2604.16548v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The emergence of writable, cross-session persistent memory in LLM agents introduces a qualitatively different threat landscape from conventional input-centric security concerns, characterized by three properties: persistence, statefulness, and propagation. To systematically characterize this landscape, we propose a Memory Lifecycle Framework that organizes attacks, defenses, and their cross-phase dependencies along two axes: six lifecycle phases (Write, Store, Retrieve, Execute, Share & Propagate, Forget & Rollback) and four security objectives (Integrity, Confidentiality, Availability, Governance). This analysis in turn exposes the need for explicit security requirements at the system level, motivating Verifiable Memory Governance (VMG), a framework of five architectural primitives for specifying and evaluating auditable, recoverable control over memory state within declared system and threat-model boundaries. Our analysis motivates integrating provenance, versioning, and policy-aware retention with retrieval and execution defenses to support auditable prevention, containment, and recovery across the lifecycle.

items.title: What Does a Harness Repair? Three Preregistered Studies Around a Longevity-Tuned Language Model
items.description: arXiv:2610.05533v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A harness search around a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7B model reported a rescue. An audit found that the gain came from rows the start left unparsed, that the caller sent each row's reference answer as an assistant turn, and that replication through the same pipeline missed it. Is a harness's gain more than a constant answer would give? We preregistered three studies and report every endpoint. In the first two, thinking off raised test accuracy over a capped thinking setting in 7 of 12 cells, mostly on rows the cap left unparsed. It was not meaningfully worse than a rescue in 7 of 9 small-model test cells or than four GEPA harnesses at 1.7B. Replication reproduced an injected defect's distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases (7 fixed by design). At 14B, two GEPA harnesses beat thinking off by 34 points on test but were not detectably above the strongest constant label, and answered "Yes" in 94.6% and 98.2% of parsed mortality answers on test. In the third study (SmolLM3-3B, base Qwen3-1.7B), GEPA beat the constant on FPB (confirmatory, both partitions); thinking off was not meaningfully worse than any BoolQ harness, and 3 of 4 MMLU-Pro searches kept their seed (the fourth inconclusive on test). On Autocast (exploratory), the harnesses were within 0.7 points of the constant and gave one label in 93.1% to 96.8% of parsed answers, both on test. On questions about the input or about knowledge (FPB, BoolQ, MMLU-Pro), GEPA beat the constant or found no clear gain over thinking off; on questions that ask for a prediction (14B mortality, descriptive; Autocast, exploratory), the harness ended near the constant and gave one label almost throughout while its gain over thinking off looked large. The constant label told the two apart wherever the gain was large. This rests on few tasks that also differ in label skew, number of labels and task type, so it is not shown to depend on the kind of question.

items.title: Transferring Peptide-Target Interaction Patterns to Small Molecules by Joint Guidance for Diffusion and Flow Matching
items.description: arXiv:2610.41322v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating small molecules to target protein-protein interactions (PPIs) remains one of the most challenging yet high-reward frontiers in drug discovery. Unlike traditional small-molecule drugs that bind to deep, well-defined pockets, PPI interfaces often comprise broad, shallow binding surfaces. A natural strategy is to leverage known peptide-target interactions, as peptide ligands provide rich interface-level constraints. However, a major algorithmic challenge is that rigid atom-level conditioning on peptide structures can over-constrain the generative space and exclude valid small-molecule solutions. To address this challenge, we present PIFT (Peptide InterFace Transfer), a novel framework that transfers peptide-target interaction patterns to small molecules through joint sampling-time guidance of masked discrete diffusion and continuous flow matching. PIFT first maps peptide-target and small-molecule-target interfaces into a shared, target-conditioned interaction space, capturing transferable interface information across molecular modalities. The resulting peptide-derived reference then jointly steers building-block logits and 3D coordinates toward peptide-compatible molecules while preserving a strong adapted molecular prior. Extensive experiments across diverse PPI targets show that the learned representation captures cross-modal interaction compatibility, while peptide guidance improves interface recovery and achieves strong docking performance and favorable molecular properties.

items.title: From Representation to Readout: Mechanistic Analysis of Membership Signals in Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.41445v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Membership inference aims to determine whether a particular example was included in a model's training data. Such membership signals are often broadly described as memorization, while the underlying mechanisms can involve both how information is represented internally and how it is accessed by the model to produce behaviors. We therefore present a mechanistic study of membership signals in large language models (LLMs). We introduce Decodable Information Score, Used Information Score, and Readout Accessibility Gap (DUG), a set of complementary measures that separately quantify membership information decodable from internal representations and the extent to which it is exposed through the model's readout. Across supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL)-based membership inference methods, membership-specific effects appear in both the amount of decodable information and readout under SFT, while under RL-based membership inference methods they appear primarily in readout. Activation patching further localizes this membership-specific effect to intermediate layers. To examine whether these findings extend to a more general RL setting, we further study reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) contamination, where the training reward is independent of the reference solution. In this setting, we find that behavioral changes can emerge without a corresponding increase in likelihood-based membership inference signals.

items.title: ORION: An Outcome-Driven LLM Advisor for RL-Based Multi-Domain 6G Slice Placement
items.description: arXiv:2610.41563v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.

items.title: Latent-Lens: Visual Perception in Small Language Models Through Latent Communication
items.description: arXiv:2610.41751v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. Recent latent-communication methods exchange states between language models. How a VLM can pass visual information to a separately pretrained text-only SLM though remains unexplored. We propose \textbf{Latent-Lens}, a lightweight codec that bridges the representation gap between a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM directly in latent space, enabling them to communicate purely through hidden states. The codec consists of a domain encoder that projects hidden states from the VLM into the SLM's embedding space, and an attention decoder formalised as a LoRA that teaches the SLM to attend to these visual prefixes, while training only ${\sim}1.6$M parameters (0.2\% of the combined model size). On visual question answering (CLEVR, GQA), Latent-Lens achieves $81.0\pm7.9$\% and $65.4\pm5.4$\%, compared with $58.3\pm5.7$\% and $61.8\pm1.0$\% for text communication with the same LoRA budget (+30.2--69.8pp relative to frozen text communication), while on image captioning (Flickr8k) it improves over the same baseline by +16.5 (+18.8 frozen). We also evaluate Latent-Lens with TinyLlama-1.1B and InternVL2-1B, which use different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.

items.title: Implicit Assumptions About Tasks in Continual Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.41792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Continual learning is the study of how a model accumulates knowledge from data received over time, rather than all at once. In practice, this is typically achieved by dividing a dataset into tasks and presenting them sequentially. Explanations of the resulting measurements take into account factors such as the similarity between segments, the rate at which the data changes and the order of presentation. Each of these factors can be defined in terms of the underlying data, the partition imposed on it, or the learner that encounters it. These levels do not necessarily coincide, and it is usually left implicit which level a reported quantity refers to. We separate these and identify which properties acquire a value at each level. In controlled teacher--student experiments, we demonstrate that partitioning the same underlying trajectory at different levels of granularity, changing the order of presentation, and varying the similarity structure of the underlying data all result in different measured outcomes. We review representative benchmarks to determine which of these properties are stated. Where the underlying data cannot be inspected, as in foundation models built on undisclosed pre-training corpora, its properties are inherited by the model's initial state, and the training applied on top of it can be described.

items.title: Accurate and Auditable ECG Classification via Visibility Graph Neural Networks
items.description: arXiv:2610.41795v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Physicians read electrocardiograms (ECGs) from waveform shape and timing, yet accurate deep-learning classifiers rarely show which waveform regions drive their predictions. We introduce LYNX-ECG, a graph neural network that represents each heartbeat as a sparse visibility graph of timestamped turning points. On CODE-Test, LYNX-ECG reaches a macro F1 score of 0.889, outperforming five baselines including the ECGFounder foundation model, while its graphs need about 14% of the storage of graphs built from every sample. Because each node maps to a specific ECG time, we can delete clinically defined waveform regions and alter beat timing to audit predictions.
